title: Work-Energy Theorem

notes: **Work done by a constant force:** $W = Fd \cos \theta$, where $F$ is the magnitude of the force, $d$ is the displacement, and $\theta$ is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Work is a scalar quantity (SI unit: joule, $J = N\cdot m$). Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement ($\theta < 90^\circ$), negative when opposite ($\theta > 90^\circ$), and zero when perpendicular ($\theta = 90^\circ$).

**Work done by a variable force:** when force varies with position, work is the area under the $F-x$ graph, or mathematically, $W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} F(x) \, dx$. For a spring force $F = -kx$, the work done by the spring when stretched from $x_1$ to $x_2$ is $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_1^2 - x_2^2)$.

**Work-energy theorem:** the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: $W_{net} = \Delta K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2$. This is one of the most powerful results in mechanics — it connects forces (through work) to motion (through kinetic energy).

**Work done by gravity:** $W_g = mg\Delta h = mg(h_i - h_f)$, where $\Delta h$ is the change in height. Gravity does positive work when the body falls ($h$ decreases) and negative work when it rises ($h$ increases). The work done by gravity is independent of the path — only the vertical displacement matters.

**Work done by a spring:** $W_s = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$ (work done ON the spring to stretch/compress it by $x$). The spring does work $W = \frac{1}{2}k(x_i^2 - x_f^2)$ when it returns from $x_i$ to $x_f$. At the natural length ($x = 0$), the spring does maximum work.

**Work done by friction:** $W_f = -f_k\cdot d = -\mu_k\cdot N\cdot d$. Friction always does negative work (it opposes motion), converting mechanical energy into heat. The work depends on the path length $d$, not just the displacement — friction is non-conservative.

**Zero work situations:** (1) Force perpendicular to displacement (e.g., normal force on a horizontal surface, centripetal force in circular motion). (2) No displacement (pushing a wall). (3) Force applied to a body that doesn't move.

**NEB exam focus:** work done by constant force ($W = Fd \cos \theta$), work done by a spring ($W = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$), work-energy theorem ($W_{net} = \Delta K$), area under $F-x$ graph for variable forces, and identifying zero-work situations.
confusion: ❌ 'Work and energy are different concepts.' ✅ Work is a TRANSFER of energy. When you do work on a body, you transfer energy to it. The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) makes this precise.
❌ 'Work is a vector because force and displacement are vectors.' ✅ Work is a SCALAR — it is the dot product of force and displacement (W = F·d·cos θ). It has magnitude but no direction.

❌ 'If a body moves, work must be done.' ✅ Work is done only if the force has a component along the displacement. Centripetal force does zero work in circular motion (always perpendicular to velocity).
❌ 'Work done by gravity depends on the path.' ✅ Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on the vertical displacement (mgΔh), not on the path taken.
❌ 'A spring does work W = ½kx² when stretched by x.' ✅ The work done ON the spring to stretch it is ½kx². The work done BY the spring when it returns is also ½kx² (energy is recovered).
❌ 'Friction always does negative work.' ✅ Static friction can do positive work — e.g., the static friction on your feet pushes you forward when walking. Kinetic friction always does negative work.

universalFacts: Work is the dot product of force and displacement — a scalar quantity measured in joules.
The work-energy theorem (W_net = ΔK) connects forces to motion and is one of the most powerful results in mechanics.
Gravity is a conservative force — work depends only on vertical displacement, not on the path.
Friction is a non-conservative force — work depends on the path length and is always negative (for kinetic friction).

examples: Constant force: A 20 N force pushes a block 5 m at 30° to the horizontal. W = 20 × 5 × cos 30° = 86.6 J.
Variable force (spring): A spring (k = 100 N/m) is stretched from 0 to 0.2 m. W = ½ × 100 × 0.2² = 2 J.
Work-energy theorem: A 2 kg block accelerates from 3 m/s to 7 m/s. W_net = ½ × 2 × (49 − 9) = 40 J.
Gravity: A 5 kg object falls 10 m. W_g = 5 × 9.8 × 10 = 490 J (positive, body speeds up).
Zero work: A body moves in a circle at constant speed. Centripetal force is perpendicular to velocity → W = 0.
practiceQuestions: A 30 N force pushes a block 10 m at 60° to the horizontal. Find the work done.
A spring (k = 200 N/m) is compressed from 0.1 m to 0.3 m. Find the work done by the spring.
A 5 kg block accelerates from 2 m/s to 8 m/s. Find the net work done.
A 3 kg object is lifted 15 m vertically. Find the work done by gravity.
A body moves in a vertical circle of radius 2 m at constant speed 4 m/s. Find the work done by the centripetal force in one complete revolution.

Friction is a non-conservative force — work depends on the path length and is always negative (for kinetic friction).
A spring stores elastic potential energy U = ½kx² when stretched or compressed — this energy is fully recoverable.
